title: What God Has Yoked Together
sum: Jesus finishes his teaching on life in the church and leaves Galilee for the last time, heading south toward Jerusalem along the east side of the Jordan (19:1–2). Pharisees test him with the most disputed marriage question of the day: may a man divorce his wife "on any ground at all"? Jesus goes back past Moses' divorce law to creation itself: God made them male and female, and the two become one flesh. Moses allowed divorce because of hard hearts, but anyone who divorces his wife, except for sexual sin, and marries another commits adultery (19:3–9). The shocked disciples say it would be better not to marry, and Jesus speaks of those who give up marriage for the kingdom (19:10–12).

He welcomes little children whom the disciples tried to turn away (19:13–15). Then a rich young man asks what good he must do to have eternal life. Jesus points him to the commandments, and when the man says he has kept them all, tells him to sell everything, give to the poor and follow him. The man leaves in grief (19:16–22). Jesus warns that a camel could get through a needle's eye more easily than a rich person into God's kingdom, yet what is impossible for people is possible for God. To Peter's question about reward he promises the Twelve thrones in the renewed world and a hundredfold return to all who leave everything for him (19:23–30).
readings: Read as household teaching

Chapters 19–20 follow the pattern of the household codes of the ancient world (husbands and wives, children, property, masters and slaves), but turn each one around: marriage is a lifelong yoke set by God, children are models of the kingdom, wealth is a danger, and greatness means slavery (20:26–28). Warren Carter set out this reading in Households and Discipleship (1994). Read this way, the chapter teaches how disciples live in families and with money.
Read as the road to the cross

From 19:1 on, Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem to die. Every teaching on the road is about giving something up: a husband's right to dismiss his wife, the disciples' sense of importance, the young man's wealth, the Twelve's claim to reward. Read this way, the chapter prepares the reader for the one who will give up his own life (20:28).
Read as Jewish debate

Each scene matches questions that Jewish teachers of the time argued: grounds for divorce (Hillel and Shammai), the meaning of "the good," which commandments lead to life, and the reward of the righteous in the world to come. Read this way, Jesus is a Jewish teacher giving strict, prophetic answers within his people's debates, not against Judaism.

views.H: The setting is Perea, the territory of Herod Antipas, who had divorced his first wife to marry his brother's wife and had executed John the Baptist for protesting (14:3–12). A question on divorce asked there had political danger. In Jewish law only a husband could divorce; Roman law allowed either spouse. Wealth in Galilee and Judea was concentrated in a few landowning families, and most people lived close to poverty. Historians widely accept that Jesus forbade divorce in some form, because the saying appears in Mark, in the material shared by Matthew and Luke, and in Paul (1 Corinthians 7:10–11).
views.C: Matthew follows Mark 10:1–31 closely but changes it. He adds "for any cause" to the question and "except for sexual sin" to the answer, which most critical scholars see as Matthew bringing Jesus' absolute ban (Mark 10:11–12; Luke 16:18) into line with the practice of his Jewish-Christian community, perhaps siding with the school of Shammai. He adds the eunuch saying (19:10–12, found only in Matthew), rewrites the rich man's question so that Jesus does not seem to deny his own goodness, and adds the twelve thrones from the material he shares with Luke (Luke 22:28–30).
views.L: 19:1 marks a turning point: the fourth discourse is over and the journey to Jerusalem begins. The chapter is framed by reversals: the "first" and "last" saying (19:30) and its mirror in 20:16 wrap the parable of the workers. The questions move from marriage to children to possessions, the main parts of an ancient household. The young man is a negative model, as the children are a positive one: those who receive, not those who achieve, enter the kingdom.
views.J: Jewish readers recognize the divorce debate from the Mishnah (Gittin 9:10), where the school of Shammai allowed divorce only for sexual misconduct and the school of Hillel for any cause. Jesus' position in Matthew is close to Shammai's, though stricter on remarriage. Rabbinic Judaism kept the get (bill of divorce) and continues to require one; Jewish tradition also says that "even the altar sheds tears" over a man who divorces the wife of his youth (Talmud, Gittin 90b). The rich man's question about the good and the commandments is a Jewish question with a Jewish answer, and Amy-Jill Levine warns against reading him as a symbol of Jewish legalism: he is a sincere Jew who keeps the Law and cannot let go of his property.
views.T: The church fathers used 19:3–9 to forbid divorce and remarriage, with the West (Augustine, Jerome) holding that adultery allowed separation but not a new marriage, and the East allowing a second marriage in some cases. 19:12 grounded the honor of celibacy and the monastic life, and 19:21 sent Antony of Egypt into the desert. 19:13–15 has long been read at infant baptisms in Lutheran and Anglican rites (in Mark's form). The saying about the camel was preached against wealth from Clement of Alexandria (Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?) to the present.

deep.b:
In Jewish law of Jesus' time a husband divorced his wife by giving her a get, a written document that said "you are free to marry any man" (Mishnah Gittin 9:3). A wife could not divorce her husband, though she could sometimes ask a court to compel him. Deuteronomy 24:1 allowed divorce when the husband found "something indecent" in his wife, and the schools of Shammai and Hillel disagreed on what that meant (see the note on 19:3). In practice the Hillelite "any cause" divorce became common, and Josephus and Philo both describe divorce for any reason as normal.

Against that background Jesus' answer was startling. He grounds marriage in creation, not in Deuteronomy's regulation; he treats remarriage after an unlawful divorce as adultery; and Matthew records one exception, porneia. In the Roman world, where Matthew's readers also lived, both husbands and wives could divorce freely. The disciples' reaction (19:10) shows how hard the teaching sounded. Some groups of Jews were also strict: the Damascus Document from the Qumran movement forbids a man to take a second wife while the first lives, citing "male and female he created them."

deep.h: Where the four New Testament texts agree and differ
deep.b: There are four sayings on divorce: Mark 10:11–12 (no exception; applies to both husband and wife), Luke 16:18 (no exception), Matthew 5:32 and 19:9 (exception for porneia), and Paul in 1 Corinthians 7:10–16, who quotes the Lord's command and then adds his own ruling for a believer whose unbelieving spouse leaves. Christians who allow remarriage after divorce usually rest their case on Matthew's exception and Paul's "not bound" (1 Corinthians 7:15). Those who forbid it point to the absolute form in Mark, Luke and Paul's "let her remain unmarried" (1 Corinthians 7:11), and read Matthew's exception narrowly. Instone-Brewer argues that first-century readers would also have assumed the grounds in Exodus 21:10–11 (neglect of food, clothing and marital love), which Jesus did not discuss. The texts can be harmonized in several ways, and churches have done so differently (see the card below).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the young man and the eunuchs
deep.b: This is my own suggestion, not a common reading. Matthew sets two kinds of "giving up" side by side in one chapter: some "make themselves eunuchs" for the kingdom (19:12), and one young man cannot give up his property (19:22). Both sayings end with a hint that only some receive the gift (19:11, "only those who have been given it"; 19:26, "with God, anything is possible"). I think Matthew means the two to be read together: the kingdom calls for different surrenders from different people, and in each case the strength to make them is given by God, not achieved. This overlaps with the common observation that 19:26 answers 19:11, but I have not found the pairing of the eunuch saying with the rich man argued at length.

echoes: Genesis 1:27; Genesis 2:24; Deuteronomy 24:1–4; Malachi 2:14–16; 5:31–32; Mark 10:1–31; Luke 16:18; Luke 18:15–30; 1 Corinthians 7:10–16; Isaiah 56:3–5; Exodus 20:12–16; Leviticus 19:18; 6:19–24; Luke 22:28–30

settings.what: The controversy over divorce
settings.to: Pharisees who came to test him, with the crowds and the disciples present
settings.when: on the road south through Perea, Herod Antipas' territory, after Jesus left Galilee
settings.why: To answer a disputed legal question (Hillel's "any cause" divorce or Shammai's narrower rule) by going behind Deuteronomy to God's purpose at creation. The question was a trap: Antipas had executed John for condemning his divorce and remarriage. Knowing that the issue was a debate between Jewish schools keeps the reader from hearing it as Jesus against "Judaism." The law at stake bound Jewish husbands, the only ones who could divorce under Jewish law.
settings.readers: For Matthew's Jewish-Christian community, likely living among synagogues and in a Roman city where either spouse could divorce, the passage set a rule for church members, and the exception clause addressed real cases of unfaithfulness.
views: Many conservative scholars hold that Jesus himself allowed the exception, and Mark and Luke give the general rule without it.
Most critical scholars think Jesus forbade divorce absolutely and Matthew's church added the exception, as Paul added his own ruling in 1 Corinthians 7:12–15.

settings.what: The saying about eunuchs for the kingdom
settings.to: his disciples, probably in private after the debate
settings.when: right after the teaching on divorce, when the disciples object that it is better not to marry
settings.why: To answer the disciples: remaining unmarried is not an escape from a hard rule but a gift and a calling some receive for the kingdom's sake. In a culture where marriage and children were a religious duty (Genesis 1:28; Mishnah Yevamot 6:6), Jesus honors the single life without commanding it.
settings.readers: For Matthew's community it gave a place to unmarried members, including missionaries who traveled without families and possibly eunuchs, who had been kept out of Israel's assembly (Deuteronomy 23:1).

settings.what: Jesus' words about the children
settings.to: the disciples who were turning the children away, in front of the parents
settings.when: on the journey, as people bring children to him for a blessing
settings.why: To correct the disciples' sense of who matters, repeating the lesson of 18:1–5: the kingdom belongs to those with no status, who receive rather than earn.
settings.readers: For the early church the scene answered how to treat children in the community, and it was later read in debates on baptizing infants.

settings.what: The conversation with the rich young man
settings.to: a wealthy young Jewish man who kept the commandments
settings.when: on the road, after the blessing of the children
settings.why: To answer a sincere question about eternal life, then to show the man the one thing standing between him and wholehearted following. The command to sell everything was addressed to him, not given as a general law.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, some of them people of means, heard a call to treat property as something to be given up when it competes with following Jesus.

settings.what: Teaching on riches and the reward of disciples
settings.to: the disciples, and Peter in particular
settings.when: as the young man walks away
settings.why: To overturn the assumption that wealth shows God's favor, to assure the disciples that salvation is God's doing, and to promise that nothing given up for him is lost. The promise of twelve thrones speaks to Israel's hope of restoration.
settings.readers: For readers who had left families, homes or synagogues to follow Jesus, it promised a new family now and eternal life to come.

traditions.q: What does 19:3–12 add to the divorce question already met at 5:32 (see the card on Matthew 5): Moses' permission, "from the beginning," and remarriage?
views: "From the beginning" shows marriage as God's original plan, which Christ restores; Moses' certificate was a concession to hardness of heart that Christ withdraws, so a valid, consummated marriage of baptized people cannot be dissolved and remarriage while the spouse lives is not allowed (Catechism 1614–1615, 2382).

"From the beginning" states the ideal of one lifelong marriage. Out of pastoral mercy ("economy") for human weakness, the Church may still bless a second marriage after divorce, with a penitential service.

Moses' certificate limited the harm a husband could do; Jesus' exception for sexual sin, read with desertion in 1 Corinthians 7:15, frees the innocent party to remarry (Luther, The Estate of Marriage, 1522).
Moses permitted divorce but did not command it; adultery, or desertion that cannot be remedied, allows the innocent party to divorce and remarry (Westminster Confession 24.5–6).

The United Methodist Social Principles call marriage a lifelong covenant and divorce a regrettable alternative when a marriage cannot be saved, and they state that divorce does not rule out a new marriage (Book of Discipline, paragraph 161).

Civil divorce and remarriage are allowed. A temple sealing, however, is not ended by civil divorce: it remains until the First Presidency cancels it, and a woman needs that cancellation before she can be sealed to another husband (General Handbook, chapter 38).

traditions.q: Is a vow of celibacy (19:12) a higher calling, and may churches require it of clergy?
views: Celibacy for the kingdom is a gift and a sign of the world to come (Catechism 1618–1620). In the Latin Church, priests are ordinarily chosen from men who commit to celibacy (Catechism 1579); Eastern Catholic churches ordain married men as priests.
Monastic celibacy is honored, and bishops are chosen from celibate clergy, but parish priests may marry before ordination and most do.
Celibacy is a gift few have; requiring it of clergy is against God's word and leads to sin. Priests may marry (Augsburg Confession 23).

Clergy may marry at their own discretion, "as they shall judge the same to serve better to godliness" (Thirty-Nine Articles 32). Religious orders of celibate men and women exist in parts of the communion.
Singleness and marriage are both callings; no vow of lifelong celibacy should be required, and none ranks above the other (Calvin, Institutes 4.12–13).

traditions.q: Does "do not stop them from coming to me" (19:14) support baptizing infants?
views: Yes. Children need the new birth of baptism and should not be kept from Christ; the church baptizes infants and entrusts children who die unbaptized to God's mercy, citing Jesus' welcome of children (Catechism 1250–1252, 1261).
Yes. Infants are baptized, chrismated and given communion, received fully into the church as Jesus received the children.
Yes. Luther's baptismal order reads this welcome of the children (in Mark's form) as Christ's own invitation to bring infants to baptism, where God gives faith.

Yes, but for a different reason than Lutherans give. Children of believers belong to God's covenant, as Israel's children did, and baptism is the sign and seal of that covenant, not the means of new birth. Calvin argued from Jesus' embrace of the children here that infants are not to be kept from the sign of Christ (Institutes 4.16.7; Westminster Confession 28.4; Heidelberg Catechism 74).
Yes. The Prayer Book's service for the baptism of infants reads Mark's account of Jesus blessing the children as warrant for the practice.
No. Jesus blessed the children; he did not baptize them. Baptism is for those who profess faith, and children are dedicated to God instead (London Confession 29; Baptist Faith and Message 7).

traditions.q: Is "sell what you own" (19:21) a counsel of perfection for some Christians, or a command for this man only?
views: Besides the commandments for all, Christ gives "evangelical counsels" of poverty, chastity and obedience, which some are called to vow in religious life as a way of perfect charity (Catechism 915, 1973–1974; Aquinas, Summa I-II q.108 a.4).
Monastics renounce property in following this call, but perfection in love is the goal of every Christian, married or monastic.

No two levels of Christians. Monastic vows that claim to merit a higher perfection are against the Gospel; the command exposed this man's idol, and every Christian is called to faith and love in daily vocation (Augsburg Confession 27; Luther, On Monastic Vows).
Wesley urged every Christian to "gain all you can, save all you can, give all you can," treating wealth beyond need as belonging to the poor; Christian perfection is a calling for all believers.

Some Anabaptist communities, such as the Hutterites, practice shared property as the normal life of the church, taking this and Acts 2:44–45 as binding on all members; most Mennonites practice mutual aid without common ownership.

title: The Last Will Be First
sum: Jesus tells a parable about a landowner who hires workers for his vineyard at dawn, mid-morning, noon, mid-afternoon and an hour before sunset, and then pays them all a full day's wage, starting with the last. Those hired first complain that the latecomers have been made equal to them. The owner answers that he has cheated no one, and asks: "Is your eye evil because I am good?" So the last will be first, and the first last (20:1–16).

On the way up to Jerusalem Jesus predicts for the third time that he will be handed over, condemned, mocked, whipped, crucified and raised (20:17–19). The mother of James and John asks for her sons to sit at his right and left in his kingdom. Jesus asks if they can drink his cup, and then teaches all twelve that among them greatness means serving, as the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many (20:20–28). Leaving Jericho, two blind men cry out to him as Son of David, and he gives them sight; they follow him on the road to Jerusalem (20:29–34).
readings: Read as a parable of grace

The landowner's pay is a gift, not a wage earned by hours. Read this way, the parable means that God's salvation is the same for all who come, whenever they come, and that resentment of others' blessing is the real danger. This is the reading of Augustine and the Reformers, and of many modern preachers.
Read as a story of the first and the last in Israel

The early workers are those who long served God (Israel, or its leaders, or the disciples), and the late ones are tax collectors, sinners and Gentiles welcomed by Jesus. Read this way, the parable answers complaints like the older brother's in Luke 15:25–32.
Read as a social picture

A rich landowner gives each day laborer enough to feed a family, whatever the market says each one deserves. Read this way, it shows the kind of justice God wants in the economy. Some readers go further and see the owner as exploiting the workers, a reading most commentators reject.

views.H: Day laborers were the poorest free workers in Roman Palestine, and the Law required that they be paid before sunset (Deuteronomy 24:14–15). Jericho, the last stop before the climb to Jerusalem, was a wealthy oasis with Herod's winter palace. The road up from Jericho rises more than 3,000 feet in about 15 miles, and Passover pilgrims took it in crowds.
views.C: The parable of the workers is found only in Matthew. The rest of the chapter follows Mark 10:32–52, with changes: the mother makes the request, "crucify" is named in the prediction, and there are two blind men instead of one (Bartimaeus). Many scholars hold that the parable goes back to Jesus, and that Matthew placed it here as a comment on Peter's question in 19:27.
views.L: 20:16 closes the frame begun at 19:30. The chapter moves from a parable of reversal to a lesson in reversal: the disciples' wish for the highest seats is answered by the Son of Man who serves. The right and left places are filled ironically at the crucifixion by two bandits (27:38). The blind men who "see" and follow are a model for the disciples, who still do not see what kind of king they follow.
views.J: Rabbinic literature has a close parallel: a king hired workers, and paid one who had worked only two hours a full day's wage, because "he did more in two hours than you in a whole day" (Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot 2:8, a eulogy for Rabbi Bun). The difference is telling: in the rabbinic story the late worker earned it; in Jesus' story the owner is simply generous. "Son of David" as a healer fits Jewish traditions about Solomon. Jewish readers note that the parable's view of grace is close to Jewish teaching that God's reward is not strictly wages (Mishnah Avot 1:3: serve not for the sake of reward).
views.T: From Irenaeus to Chrysostom and Gregory the Great, the fathers read the hours as the ages of history or the stages of a person's life. The parable became a comfort to those converted late in life. 20:28 was central to the church's teaching on the atonement, and the phrase "ransom for many" is echoed in the eucharistic words of 26:28. The blind men's cry, Kyrie eleison, entered the liturgy, and "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me" became the Jesus Prayer of the Orthodox tradition.

deep.b: 20:28 is one of the few places where Jesus in the first three Gospels says why he will die. Its words draw on Isaiah 53, where the LORD's servant "bore the sin of many" and makes himself an offering for guilt (Isaiah 53:10–12), and on the language of buying back slaves and captives. Christians have explained it in several ways. The early church fathers spoke of Christ ransoming humanity from death and the devil's power; some, like Origen, asked to whom the price was paid, while others, like Gregory of Nazianzus, warned against pressing the picture. Anselm (about 1098) explained the death as satisfaction of God's honor, and the Reformers as Christ bearing the penalty of sin in our place. Others stress Christ's victory over evil (the "Christus Victor" view of Gustaf Aulén) or his example of self-giving love. All of these use this verse. In its setting, the point is first ethical: the disciples must serve, because their master gives himself.

settings.what: The parable of the workers in the vineyard
settings.to: the disciples, answering Peter's question "What will there be for us?" (19:27)
settings.when: on the road to Jerusalem, right after the rich young man leaves
settings.why: To warn the Twelve, who have left everything and expect reward, against counting their service as a claim on God or resenting others who receive the same grace. Knowing that it answers Peter changes the reading: it is not first about Jews and Gentiles, but about the disciples' own attitude.
settings.readers: Matthew's mixed church of long-time Jewish believers and newer Gentile members could hear in it a warning against ranking members by seniority.
views: Most commentators follow Matthew's setting: a lesson for disciples about reward.
Joachim Jeremias argued that in Jesus' ministry the parable first defended his welcome of sinners against critics such as the Pharisees, as in Luke 15.

settings.what: The third prediction of the passion
settings.to: the Twelve, taken aside from the crowd of pilgrims
settings.when: on the road up to Jerusalem before Passover
settings.why: To prepare his closest followers for what will happen in the city, so that the coming events will not destroy their faith, and to show that he goes to his death knowingly.
settings.readers: Readers who knew the end of the story heard proof that Jesus was not a victim of events but walked into them on purpose.

settings.what: The request for the best seats and the teaching on greatness
settings.to: the mother of James and John and her sons, then all twelve disciples
settings.when: on the road, just after the passion prediction
settings.why: To expose ambition among the Twelve and to redefine greatness in the kingdom as service, after the pattern of the Son of Man, who gives his life for many. In a society ruled by honor and patronage, this reversed the ladder of status.
settings.readers: For church leaders in Matthew's community and after, it was the charter of Christian leadership as service (compare 23:8–12).

settings.what: The blind men's cry and Jesus' question
settings.to: Jesus, in front of the crowd leaving Jericho
settings.when: on the last stage of the journey, leaving Jericho, shortly before the entry into Jerusalem
settings.why: The men's cry to the "Son of David" announces, just before the entry, who Jesus is. Jesus' question ("What would you like me to do for you?") echoes his question to the mother of Zebedee's sons (20:21): these men ask for sight, not seats of honor.
settings.readers: For Matthew's readers the healed men who "followed him" model true discipleship.

title: Your King Is Coming
sum: Near Jerusalem Jesus sends two disciples for a donkey and her colt, and rides into the city as Zechariah had foretold: a gentle king on a donkey. Crowds spread cloaks and branches on the road and shout "Hosanna to the Son of David!" from Psalm 118. The whole city is shaken and asks, "Who is this?" (21:1–11). In the temple Jesus drives out the sellers and money changers, quoting Isaiah and Jeremiah, heals the blind and the lame, and defends the children who praise him (21:12–17). The next morning he finds a fig tree with leaves but no fruit, and it withers at his word, a sign that becomes a lesson on faith (21:18–22).

Back in the temple the chief priests and elders demand to know his authority. He answers with a question about John's baptism they will not answer (21:23–27). Then he tells two parables against them. In the first, a son who refuses his father but later goes to work is contrasted with one who says yes and never goes: tax collectors and prostitutes are entering God's kingdom ahead of the leaders (21:28–32). In the second, tenants of a vineyard beat and kill the owner's slaves and finally his son; the kingdom will be taken from them and given to a nation that yields its fruit, for the rejected stone has become the head of the corner (21:33–46).
readings: Read as a royal arrival

Ancient cities welcomed kings and generals with processions, songs and garments on the road. Jesus enters Jerusalem as a king, but on a donkey, not a war horse, and his first act is not to seize the palace but to cleanse the temple and heal. Read this way, the chapter shows what kind of king he is.
Read as prophetic signs

Like Jeremiah and Ezekiel, Jesus acts out his message: the ride, the overturned tables, the withered tree. Each is a sign of judgment on the temple and its leaders, and the parables at the end spell it out. Read this way, the chapter is about the end of the temple order, which came in AD 70.
Read through Psalm 118

The crowds sing Psalm 118:25–26 at the entry, the children repeat it in the temple, and Jesus ends the chapter by quoting Psalm 118:22–23 about the rejected stone. Read this way, the whole chapter is a festival psalm come true: the one who comes in the Lord's name is rejected by the builders and made the cornerstone.

views.H: Jesus came to Jerusalem for Passover, when the city's population swelled with pilgrims and Roman troops stood on alert. The temple was Herod's great rebuilding, still under construction; its outer court hosted the market for sacrificial animals and the exchange of coins for the temple tax. Most historians accept that Jesus caused a disturbance in the temple and that it led directly to his arrest (Sanders). Whether the entry was as public as the Gospels say is debated, since the Romans did not arrest him at once.
views.C: Matthew follows Mark 11–12 but tightens it: the temple cleansing happens on the day of entry, the fig tree withers at once, and Matthew adds the two animals, the Zechariah quotation, the healing and the children in the temple (21:14–16), the parable of the two sons (only in Matthew), and the saying about the kingdom being taken away (21:43). Many critical scholars see in 21:43 and 22:7 the experience of Matthew's community after AD 70, as it defined itself against the synagogue leadership.
views.L: The chapter begins the last week in Jerusalem and a series of conflicts in the temple that runs to the end of chapter 23. Matthew's fulfillment formula (21:4) marks the entry as Scripture fulfilled. Three parables (two sons, tenants, wedding feast, 21:28–22:14) form a set aimed at the leaders. The question "Who is this?" (21:10) is answered by the crowds ("the prophet"), by the children ("Son of David"), and by the parable ("his own son").
views.J: Jewish readers note that the crowds who welcome Jesus are Jews, as are the blind, the lame and the children who praise him; the conflict is with the temple leadership, not with the Jewish people. Zechariah 9:9 was read as messianic in rabbinic tradition (Talmud, Sanhedrin 98a). The parable of the tenants has often been used to teach that God rejected Israel; Jewish and Christian scholars today (Levine, Saldarini) argue that in Matthew it targets the leaders who "understood that he meant them" (21:45). Josephus and the Talmud also criticize the high priestly families of the period for greed and violence (Talmud, Pesachim 57a).
views.T: The entry is celebrated on Palm Sunday, with processions of branches from at least the late 300s in Jerusalem (described by the pilgrim Egeria). "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord" is sung in the Sanctus at the Eucharist. The cleansing of the temple was used by reformers of every age against corruption in the church. The parable of the tenants, read in the fathers as the story of Israel's rejection and the Gentiles' calling, has been reread since the Holocaust in light of statements such as Nostra Aetate.

deep.h: The kingdom taken away: how 21:43 has been read
deep.b:
Only Matthew has 21:43. For most of church history it was read as a verdict on the Jewish people: God took the kingdom from Israel and gave it to the Gentile church. Justin Martyr's Dialogue with Trypho, Chrysostom's sermons and many later writers argued this way; Luther, in On the Jews and Their Lies (1543), went further and urged violence against Jews. Catholic practice, too, long carried the replacement reading, for example in the Good Friday prayer "for the faithless Jews" (pro perfidis Judaeis), whose wording was changed only in 1959–1962. The reading supported the idea that the church had replaced Israel (supersessionism) and, at its worst, contempt for Jews. In the decades after the Holocaust, many churches reexamined such readings. Vatican II's Nostra Aetate (1965) taught that the Jews "should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God, as if this followed from the holy Scriptures," and many Protestant bodies issued similar statements, such as the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America's repudiation of Luther's anti-Jewish writings (1994).

In the text, Jesus speaks to the chief priests and elders, and Matthew notes that "the chief priests and the Pharisees... understood that he meant them" (21:45). The "you" is first of all Israel's leaders, the tenants entrusted with God's vineyard. The "nation" (ethnos) that bears fruit is not called "the Gentiles" (that would be plural); for Matthew it is the community of Jesus' followers, Jews first and then people of all nations (28:19). Scholars still disagree on how much Matthew saw his church as a new people replacing the old and how much as faithful Israel renewed. Readers should know both the long history of the replacement reading and the strong reasons, from the text itself, for reading it more narrowly.

deep.h: Why did Jesus overturn the tables?
deep.b: Three main answers are given. Reform: Jesus protested commerce or cheating in a holy place, restoring it to prayer (the traditional view; Jeremiah 7:11 accuses the people of using the temple as a hideout). Inclusion: the market filled the one court where Gentiles could pray, and Mark's quotation "for all the nations" (Mark 11:17) points that way, though Matthew omits it. Sign of destruction: E. P. Sanders argued that the trade was necessary for sacrifice and not corrupt in itself, so overturning it was a prophetic sign that God would destroy the temple and build a new one, which fits the charge at Jesus' trial (26:61). Many scholars combine these. Matthew's own additions, healing the blind and lame and the children's praise, show the temple being restored to what it was for.

echoes: Zechariah 9:9; Isaiah 62:11; Psalm 118:22–26; Isaiah 56:7; Jeremiah 7:11; Psalm 8:2; 2 Samuel 5:8; Hosea 9:10; Isaiah 5:1–7; Daniel 2:34–35; Isaiah 8:14–15; Mark 11:1–12:12; Luke 19:28–48; Luke 20:1–19; John 2:13–22; John 12:12–19; Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:7

settings.what: The entry into Jerusalem and the crowds' acclamation
settings.by: Jesus' instructions to two disciples; the crowds' songs from Psalm 118
settings.to: the disciples; then the city of Jerusalem, crowded with Passover pilgrims
settings.when: traditionally Palm Sunday, the Sunday before Passover (the day comes from John 12:1, 12, not Matthew), as Jesus arrives from Jericho over the Mount of Olives
settings.why: Jesus' acted message, riding a donkey, claims Zechariah's promise of a humble king of peace, not a warrior. The crowds' Hosanna hails him as David's heir. The city's question "Who is this?" sets up the conflicts of the next days.
settings.readers: For Matthew's readers, probably after AD 70 (the view of most critical scholars), the scene showed Jerusalem welcoming its king and then, through its leaders, rejecting him; the fulfillment quotation assured them that this was Scripture fulfilled.

settings.what: Jesus' words in the temple
settings.to: the sellers and money changers, then the chief priests and scribes
settings.when: on arrival in the city, in the temple's outer court
settings.why: To condemn the use of the temple, quoting Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11, and to defend the children's praise with Psalm 8. The sayings call the temple back to prayer and warn, through Jeremiah, of its destruction. The rule at stake is not the Torah's sacrifices themselves but how the temple was being run.
settings.readers: For readers after the temple's fall the scene explained that judgment had been announced in advance.
views: Jesus objected to commerce in the sacred place.

settings.what: The cursing of the fig tree and the saying on faith
settings.to: the disciples
settings.when: the next morning, on the road from Bethany into the city
settings.why: A prophetic sign of judgment on fruitlessness, like the prophets' symbolic acts, turned into a lesson that faith and prayer can do what seems impossible.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, who saw the temple destroyed, could read the sign as judgment fulfilled and the promise as encouragement to pray.

settings.what: The controversy over Jesus' authority
settings.by: Jesus, answering the chief priests and elders
settings.to: the chief priests and the elders of the people
settings.when: in the temple courts, where Jesus was teaching, the day after he overturned the tables
settings.why: The temple authorities ask by what right he acts in their temple. Jesus links his authority to John's, whom the people held to be a prophet, and exposes their unwillingness to judge honestly.
settings.readers: For Matthew's readers it showed that the leaders had rejected both God's messengers, John and Jesus.

settings.what: The parable of the two sons
settings.to: the chief priests and elders, in the temple
settings.when: right after their refusal to answer about John
settings.why: To make the leaders judge themselves: doing the father's will matters more than saying yes. Tax collectors and prostitutes who turned at John's preaching are ahead of leaders who said yes to God in word.
settings.readers: For Matthew's community it reinforced that deeds, not words, show true obedience (7:21).

settings.what: The parable of the tenants of the vineyard
settings.to: the chief priests and elders, overheard by the Pharisees and the crowds
settings.when: in the temple, the same day
settings.why: Retelling Isaiah's song of the vineyard, Jesus charges the leaders entrusted with Israel with rejecting God's messengers and now the son, and warns that their stewardship will be taken away. Knowing that it was aimed at the leaders, who "understood that he meant them," guards against reading it as God's rejection of the Jewish people.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, probably writing after AD 70 (the view of most critical scholars), saw the vineyard given to new tenants, the community of Jesus' followers, and the leadership of the old temple judged.
views: The parable judges Israel's leaders; the vineyard (Israel) remains (Saldarini, Levine).
The traditional reading: the kingdom passed from Israel to the church (many church fathers).

traditions.q: Does 21:43 mean the church has replaced Israel as God's people?
views: No. The church is the new people of God, yet "the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God, as if this followed from the holy Scriptures"; God's gifts and call to Israel are irrevocable (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 839).

Covenant theology sees one people of God across both Testaments; the church, Jews and Gentiles together, is the continuation of Israel, and 21:43 marks the transfer of the kingdom from unbelieving leaders and people to the believing community. Many Reformed churches also affirm a future turning of Jewish people to Christ (Romans 11).

No. Israel and the church are distinct, and God's promises to national Israel will yet be fulfilled. Dispensational interpreters read 21:43 as taking the kingdom from the generation that rejected Jesus, not from Israel forever; some take the "nation" to be a future, believing Israel (Stanley Toussaint), others the church in the present age (John Walvoord).

Lutheran churches today read 21:43 as judgment on the leaders who rejected Jesus and as a call to the church to bear fruit, not as God's rejection of the Jewish people. The Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (1994) repudiated Luther's anti-Jewish writings and their later use, and committed itself to oppose all hatred of Jews.

The church, Jews and Gentiles in Christ, is the new Israel. Church fathers such as Chrysostom read the verse as the kingdom passing to the church of the nations, a reading Orthodox writers generally keep, while many today reject hostility to the Jewish people as contrary to the Gospel.

title: Give God What Is God's
sum: Jesus tells a third parable against the leaders: a king gives a wedding feast for his son, but the invited guests refuse, mistreat and kill his slaves. The king's army destroys them and burns their city, and the hall is filled with people gathered from the roads, bad and good. A guest without wedding clothes is thrown out into the darkness: the called are many, but the chosen are few (22:1–14).

Then come three tests and a counter-question. Pharisees and Herodians ask whether it is permitted to pay the head tax to Caesar; Jesus asks whose image is on the coin and says, "Pay back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God" (22:15–22). Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, tell of a woman married in turn to seven brothers; Jesus answers that in the resurrection people do not marry, and that God, who called himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, is God of the living (22:23–33). A Pharisee lawyer asks which commandment is great; Jesus names love of God with all one's being and love of neighbor as oneself, on which the whole law hangs (22:34–40). Finally Jesus asks the Pharisees how the Messiah can be David's son if David calls him "Lord" in Psalm 110. No one can answer, and no one dares question him again (22:41–46).
readings: Read as a contest

Each group of leaders tries to trap Jesus in front of the crowds, and each fails. Read this way, the chapter shows Jesus as the master teacher of the Law in the temple itself, silencing all challengers before he goes to his death.
Read as teaching on the two loyalties

The coin, the resurrection and the great commandment all ask what humans owe God. Read this way, the chapter's center is 22:21 and 22:37: everything belongs to God, who must be loved with the whole self, and that love shows itself in love of neighbor.
Read as a portrait of the Messiah
The chapter begins with the king's son and ends with David's Lord. Read this way, it is about who Jesus is: the son for whom the feast is held, and the Lord seated at God's right hand.

views.H: The tax question had a violent history: Judas the Galilean's revolt against the census of AD 6. The Herodians supported the Herod family's cooperation with Rome; the Pharisees were wary of both. The Sadducees, linked to the high priestly families, denied the resurrection and accepted only the written Law as binding. Debates about the greatest commandment and about the Messiah's descent were real topics among Jewish teachers. The coin was probably a silver denarius of Tiberius.
views.C: The wedding feast has a parallel in Luke 14:16–24 and Gospel of Thomas 64; Matthew's form adds the king, the son, the destruction of the city and the wedding garment, which many scholars see as Matthew's allegory of salvation history and judgment after AD 70. 22:15–46 follows Mark 12:13–37 closely, but Matthew turns Mark's friendly scribe (Mark 12:28–34) into a Pharisee lawyer who tests Jesus, and adds "the whole law and the Prophets hang" on the two commandments.
views.L: The wedding feast completes the three parables against the leaders begun in 21:28. Four questions follow in a set (tax, resurrection, commandment, David's son), the last asked by Jesus himself, and the series ends with total silence (22:46). The word "image" (22:20) recalls Genesis 1:27, already quoted at 19:4. The chapter prepares for the woes of chapter 23.
views.J: Jesus' answers place him within Jewish debate: like the Pharisees he affirms the resurrection against the Sadducees, and his summary of the Law in two commands matches Hillel's Golden Rule and Akiva's "great principle" (Leviticus 19:18). Rabbinic Judaism later also found the resurrection in the Torah (Talmud, Sanhedrin 90b). Jewish readers often observe that in Mark the scribe and Jesus agree warmly, and that Matthew's sharper framing reflects later conflict.
views.T: 22:21 became the classic text for relations between church and state, from Tertullian and Ambrose to Luther's two kingdoms and modern debates on religious freedom. 22:30 shaped teaching on virginity and the life to come, and 22:37–40 has been called the summary of all Christian ethics (Augustine: "Love, and do what you will"). Psalm 110:1, quoted in 22:44, is the root of the creed's "seated at the right hand of the Father."

deep.b:
The question "Is it permitted to pay the head tax to Caesar?" was designed to force Jesus to choose between collaboration and revolt. His answer avoids both traps. By asking for the coin he shows that his questioners carry Caesar's image, with its claim of divine descent, even in the temple courts. "Pay back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar" admits that a coin stamped with Caesar's face can go back to Caesar. "Give God what is God's" is the sting: what bears God's image is the human being (Genesis 1:26–27), so the whole person belongs to God.

Readers have drawn very different conclusions. Some see two realms, each with its own rights (Luther's "two kingdoms"). Some see a strict limit on the state: Caesar may have coins, never worship or conscience (Tertullian; the early martyrs who refused to sacrifice to the emperor). Some see a call to resist unjust rule, since everything belongs to God. Anabaptists read it with Jesus' call to non-violence, paying taxes while refusing the sword. See the card below.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a ring of images
deep.b: This is my own reading, offered as a suggestion. Matthew 19–22 returns twice to Genesis 1, "male and female he made them" (19:4, from Genesis 1:27) and the coin's "image" (22:20, the Greek word eikōn of Genesis 1:26–27 in the Septuagint), and then to the great commandment to love God with all one's being (22:37). I suspect Matthew wants the reader to connect them: the human being, made male and female in God's image, owes God the whole self, which is why marriage cannot be dissolved at a man's will and why Caesar's claim stops at the coin. The image-of-God reading of 22:20–21 is old (Tertullian) and common; linking it to 19:4 as a deliberate pattern is my own suggestion.

echoes: Isaiah 25:6–9; Luke 14:16–24; Revelation 19:7–9; Mark 12:13–37; Luke 20:20–44; Romans 13:1–7; Deuteronomy 25:5–10; Tobit 3:8; Exodus 3:6; Deuteronomy 6:4–5; Leviticus 19:18; Luke 10:25–28; Psalm 110:1; Acts 2:34–36; Hebrews 1:13

settings.what: The parable of the wedding feast
settings.to: the chief priests and Pharisees, in the temple, with the crowds listening
settings.when: the same day as the parable of the tenants
settings.why: To warn the leaders that refusing God's invitation has consequences, and that the feast will be filled with others; and to warn everyone who accepts that the invitation calls for a fitting life.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, probably writing after AD 70 (the view of most critical scholars), could see the burned city as Jerusalem, and the mixed crowd in the hall as their own church, called to be ready for the judgment.
views: Many scholars think Matthew and Luke preserve two versions of one parable, Matthew's turned into an allegory.
Others think Jesus told similar stories on different occasions, at a Pharisee's meal (Luke) and in the temple (Matthew).

settings.what: The question about the tax to Caesar
settings.to: disciples of the Pharisees together with the Herodians
settings.when: in the temple courts, during the last week
settings.why: The question tried to make Jesus either a collaborator or a rebel. His answer limits Caesar's claim to what bears his image and puts the whole person under God.
settings.readers: Christians in the Roman empire, who paid taxes but could not worship the emperor, found here a rule for their own situation.

settings.what: The question about the resurrection
settings.to: Sadducees, who denied the resurrection
settings.when: the same day
settings.why: The Sadducees mock belief in resurrection with a case drawn from the levirate law. Jesus answers from the Torah they accepted, showing that resurrection life is different from this life and that God's covenant faithfulness to the patriarchs requires it.
settings.readers: For Matthew's readers it confirmed the resurrection hope at the heart of their faith, argued from Scripture.

settings.what: The question about the great commandment
settings.to: a Pharisee lawyer, testing him, with other Pharisees gathered
settings.when: after Jesus silenced the Sadducees
settings.why: To answer a known question of Jewish teaching by joining Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18 and making them the hinge of all Scripture. The law at stake is the whole Torah, binding every Israelite.
settings.readers: Matthew's Jewish-Christian readers learned how to read the Law: through love, without setting any commandment aside (5:17–19).

settings.what: Jesus' question about David's son
settings.to: the Pharisees, still gathered
settings.when: the last exchange of the day, ending the questions
settings.why: To show that the Messiah is more than a son of David, a king like David; he is David's Lord, seated at God's right hand.
settings.readers: For Matthew's readers, who confessed Jesus as Son of David and Lord, the riddle explained how both could be true.

traditions.q: What does "Pay back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar" require of Christians toward the state?
views: Citizens must pay taxes and support legitimate authority, but are obliged in conscience not to follow civil laws that contradict the moral order or the Gospel; "we must obey God rather than men" (Catechism 2238–2242).

Byzantine tradition spoke of a "symphony" between church and emperor, each serving God in its own sphere. Orthodox churches today accept the modern state and pray for its rulers, but teach that when the state demands apostasy or grave sin, the church must refuse to obey (Russian Orthodox Church, Basis of the Social Concept, section 3).

God rules the world through two governments: the spiritual by the Gospel, the temporal by law and the sword. Christians serve in both, obey rulers in temporal matters, and refuse only when commanded to sin (Luther, Temporal Authority; Augsburg Confession 16).

Civil rulers are ordained by God, and Christians owe them taxes, honor and obedience in lawful things; rulers may not interfere with the preaching of the Word, and Reformed thinkers developed a right of lesser magistrates to resist tyranny (Westminster Confession 23; Calvin, Institutes 4.20).

Christians pay taxes and pray for rulers, but the sword is "outside the perfection of Christ"; believers do not serve as magistrates or soldiers (Schleitheim Confession 6). Most Mennonites today keep the commitment to non-violence.

Church and state should be separate; the state owes every church freedom, and Christians owe the state loyalty in all that is not contrary to God's revealed will (Baptist Faith and Message, article 17).

traditions.q: Does marriage continue after the resurrection (22:30)?
views: No. Marriage belongs to this present age; in the resurrection people do not marry, and consecrated virginity is a sign of that coming world (Catechism 1619–1620). Love and communion with the saints, including a spouse, are not lost.
Marriage as an institution ends, but the bond of love sanctified in it is meant to be eternal; for this reason the church has traditionally discouraged remarriage after a spouse's death.
Yes, for marriages sealed by priesthood authority in a temple "for time and all eternity"; Jesus' words describe those who were not so sealed (Doctrine and Covenants 132:15–20).
No. The resurrection life fulfills and surpasses earthly marriage; believers will know and love one another, but not as husband and wife.

title: Woe to You, and Jerusalem, Jerusalem
sum: Jesus turns to the crowds and his disciples. The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses' seat, so do what they say, but not what they do, for they say and do not do. They load heavy burdens on others, do their deeds to be seen, and love the best seats and the title "Rabbi." Jesus' followers are not to be called Rabbi, father or leader: they have one Teacher, one Father and one Leader, the Messiah, and the greatest will be a servant (23:1–12).

Then come seven woes on the scribes and Pharisees, called hypocrites: they shut the kingdom, make converts worse than themselves, play games with oaths, tithe herbs while neglecting justice, mercy and faithfulness, clean the outside of the cup, look like whitewashed tombs, and build monuments to the prophets their fathers killed. Jesus says he will send them prophets and wise men whom they will persecute, and that all the righteous blood from Abel to Zechariah will come on this generation (23:13–36). The chapter ends with a lament: Jerusalem, killer of prophets, would not be gathered like chicks under a hen's wings; its house is left deserted, and it will not see him again until it says, "Blessed is the one who comes in the Lord's name!" (23:37–39).
readings: Read as prophetic speech

The woes follow the form of the prophets' woes (Isaiah 5; Habakkuk 2). Prophets spoke harshly to their own people out of love, and the chapter ends in grief. Read this way, it is the speech of a Jewish prophet to Jewish leaders, like Amos or Jeremiah, not an attack on Judaism.
Read in Matthew's own time

After AD 70 the Pharisees' successors were becoming the leaders of the synagogues, and Matthew's Jewish-Christian community was in bitter conflict with them. Read this way, the chapter reflects that family quarrel, and its sharpness says as much about the conflict as about the Pharisees of Jesus' day.
Read as a mirror for the church

23:8–12 is addressed to Jesus' own followers, and the faults named (seeking honor, burdening others, outward religion) are temptations for any religious leader. Read this way, the chapter is first a warning to Christians, as many preachers from Chrysostom onward have said.

views.H: The Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the Law, especially purity, tithing and the Sabbath, and to the "traditions of the elders." Josephus says they were popular with ordinary people and had about six thousand members (Antiquities 17.42; 18.15). The scribes were professional experts in the Law, some of them Pharisees. Historians agree that Jesus argued with Pharisees on purity and Sabbath, but most think the full set of woes in this form, especially its sharpest charges, owes much to later conflict.
views.C: Matthew combines Mark 12:38–40 (a short warning about scribes) with a longer series of woes shared with Luke 11:39–52, where they are spoken at a Pharisee's dinner, and adds material of his own (23:2–3, 8–10, 15, 16–22). Most critical scholars date Matthew after AD 70 and read the chapter in the setting of the conflict between his community and the emerging rabbinic leadership (Saldarini, Overman). Others stress that much of the material goes back to Jesus.
views.L: Chapter 23 serves as a bridge: it closes the temple conflicts that began in 21:23 and opens the fifth great discourse (chapters 24–25), which begins as Jesus leaves the temple (24:1). The seven woes mirror the Beatitudes of chapter 5 as their dark counterpart. The chapter moves from instruction (23:1–12) to accusation (23:13–36) to lament (23:37–39).
views.J: Jewish scholars have long pointed out that the picture of the Pharisees here is a caricature if taken as a description of all Pharisees. Rabbinic sources themselves criticize hypocrisy and list seven kinds of false "Pharisees" (Talmud, Sotah 22b), and they honor sincerity and humility. Many of the practices criticized, such as tefillin, tassels, tithing and oath rules, are commands or careful applications of the Torah. Amy-Jill Levine and others urge Christians to read the chapter as internal Jewish criticism and to stop using "Pharisee" as a synonym for hypocrite.
views.T: The fathers used the chapter to warn clergy against pride (Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew 72–74) but also, too often, to attack Jews as a people (Chrysostom's sermons Against the Jews, Melito's Peri Pascha). The lament over Jerusalem became part of Holy Week. Since the 1960s many churches have issued guidelines warning preachers against using Matthew 23 to portray Judaism as legalistic or Jews as hypocrites.

deep.b:
The Pharisees (Hebrew perushim, probably "separated ones") appear in the 100s BC as a movement within Judaism. Josephus, who says he followed their way, describes them as the most accurate interpreters of the Law, who believed in fate together with free will, in the resurrection, and in reward and punishment after death, and who were influential with the common people (Antiquities 13.297–298; 18.12–15; War 2.162–163). They kept the traditions of the elders, unwritten rulings that applied the Law to daily life. They differed from the Sadducees, who rejected those traditions and the resurrection, and from the Essenes, who withdrew into separate communities.

Paul called himself "a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees" (Acts 23:6; Philippians 3:5), and Acts shows Pharisees defending the apostles (Acts 5:34–39). After AD 70 the sages who shaped rabbinic Judaism at Yavneh were largely their heirs, though the relation is debated. In the Gospels Pharisees are Jesus' chief conversation partners and critics, often because they were closest to him in belief: both cared intensely about how to live the Law. Matthew's harsh portrait should be read with this in mind. The best of Pharisaic teaching, as preserved in the rabbis, prized humility, sincerity and love of neighbor.

Chapter 23 is among the harshest passages in the New Testament. Its first setting is a debate between Jews: Jesus, a Jewish prophet, addresses Jewish teachers, and Matthew, probably a Jewish Christian, writes for a community in conflict with the synagogue's leaders. Within Judaism such sharp criticism had a long history, from Amos and Jeremiah to the Dead Sea Scrolls, which call a group most scholars identify as the Pharisees "seekers of smooth things." Ancient rhetoric between rival schools was often far harsher than modern speech.

Once the church became mostly Gentile and then powerful, the words were heard differently: as Christians condemning Jews. "Pharisee" became a byword for hypocrite in European languages, and preachers used the woes and the "blood" of 23:35 to portray Jews as killers of the prophets and of Christ. Such readings fed contempt and violence. After the Holocaust, the Catholic Church (Nostra Aetate, 1965, and the Pontifical Biblical Commission, 2001) and many Protestant churches rejected the use of these texts against Jews. Reading the chapter honestly means keeping both facts: Jesus' warning against religious hypocrisy is real and applies to every religious community, including the church; and the chapter was never meant as a charge against a whole people. Many scholars, Jewish and Christian, judge that taken as a portrait of all Pharisees or of Judaism it is unfair; others, such as R. T. France and Craig Keener, hold that the woes target specific practices and leaders, and accurately, without claiming to describe every Pharisee.

settings.what: Warnings about the scribes and Pharisees, and the rule for disciples
settings.to: the crowds and his disciples, in the temple courts
settings.when: the last day of public teaching in the temple, after the questions of chapter 22
settings.why: To warn his hearers against the teachers' example while respecting their teaching office, and to give his own followers a rule of equality: no titles that set one disciple above others, because they have one Teacher, one Father and one Leader.
settings.readers: Matthew's community, defining itself against synagogue leaders who were taking the title "rabbi," heard a rule for its own leaders (compare 20:25–28).

settings.what: The seven woes
settings.to: the scribes and Pharisees, addressed directly, with the crowds and disciples present
settings.when: the same day, in the temple, just before Jesus leaves it for the last time (24:1)
settings.why: In the prophets' form of woe, to denounce religious practice that keeps the outward details of the Law while neglecting justice, mercy and faithfulness, and to announce the judgment that will fall on that generation and the temple. The practices named (tithing, purity of vessels, oaths, tefillin, tassels) were applications of the Torah binding on Jews; Jesus does not reject them (23:23) but attacks their misuse.
settings.readers: For Matthew's readers, probably after AD 70 (the view of most critical scholars),, in conflict with the synagogue's leaders, the woes explained their rejection and the temple's fall. Later Gentile readers, who stood outside that family quarrel, often turned the words against all Jews, a misuse modern churches reject.
views: Many scholars hold that the core woes go back to Jesus' disputes with Pharisees and scribes.
Others, such as Saldarini and Overman, think the chapter's form and sharpness come largely from the post-70 conflict.

settings.what: The lament over Jerusalem
settings.to: Jerusalem, addressed as a person, in the hearing of the crowds
settings.when: at the end of his public teaching, as he prepares to leave the temple
settings.why: To grieve over the city that refused him, announce that the temple will be abandoned, and leave open the hope that Jerusalem will one day welcome him with Psalm 118's blessing. The lament shows that the woes come from grief, not hatred.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, after the city's fall, heard both the judgment fulfilled and a hope still pending.
views: Jerusalem will acknowledge him only when it is too late.
Israel will welcome its Messiah, as Romans 11:26 hopes (Allison).

traditions.q: Does "Do not call anyone on earth your father" (23:9) forbid calling clergy "Father"?
views: No. Jesus forbids putting any human in God's place, not all use of the word; Paul calls himself a father in the gospel (1 Corinthians 4:15). Priests are called "Father" as spiritual fathers who serve under the one Father.
No. Priests and bishops are addressed as "Father," and the early teachers are honored as the Church Fathers, as spiritual fathers in Christ.
Yes, in spirit. Friends refused honorific titles and "vain" forms of address as against Christ's command and the equality of all believers (Robert Barclay, Apology, proposition 15).
Most Baptists do not use "Father" for pastors and read 23:8–10 as a warning against clerical titles and hierarchy, though they do not forbid all titles ("Pastor," "Reverend").
